name: Filtered / spring water

lead: Some people drink filtered or bottled spring water instead of tap water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, hoping for cleaner skin, hair and teeth.

Spring water is groundwater emerging naturally from an aquifer, with dissolved mineral content that varies. Tap water in developed countries is described as heavily tested, and bottled water is regulated as a packaged food in the US. No human study has tested it for skin or facial appearance.

paras: People install carbon or membrane filters at home, or buy bottled spring water, for drinking and cooking. It is a standing household habit.

Some springs contain arsenic above the WHO 10 ppb standard, bottled water has been found to contain microplastics, and poorly maintained filters have been linked to outbreaks. Bottled water costs much more than tap.

chain: Filter or spring water in place of tap
angle.text: Some people drink filtered or bottled spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, aiming for cleaner skin, hair and teeth. Tap water is heavily regulated and no study has looked at appearance.

lead: Filtered or spring water is drinking water treated with a home filter or bought bottled from a spring, used by some people in place of tap water to avoid fluoride and chlorine.

Spring water is groundwater emerging naturally from an aquifer; its dissolved mineral content varies, and some springs contain arsenic above the WHO 10 ppb standard.[1] Tap water in developed countries is described as heavily tested, and bottled water is regulated as a packaged food in the US.[2] No published study was found testing filtered or spring water for facial appearance.

paras: Minerals dissolve as water passes through rock, measured as total dissolved solids; mineral water is defined as at least 250 ppm.[1] Home filters include granular activated carbon, carbon block and membrane types.[3]
In the EU, mineral and spring water are separate categories under Directive 2009/54/EC, and in the US the label must state the water type.[2]

sections.h: Regulation and comparison with tap water
paras: The FDA regulates bottled water as a packaged food with rules at least as strict as the EPA's tap water standards.[2] One Cincinnati study found bacterial counts in some bottled water above those in tap water, and a 2018 study reported microplastics in the large majority of bottled brands tested.[2] Bottled water costs far more per gallon, and some is municipal tap water.[2]
Springs are not always safe to drink and require testing.[1] A 2007 camp outbreak of giardiasis followed installation of a slow-sand filtration system containing unsterilised sand.[4]

Practitioners cite avoiding fluoride and chlorine as the motive. Water filters on the sources reviewed are not described as removing fluoride or chlorine, and published research on appearance outcomes was not found.

No studies found on filtered or spring water for facial appearance. A laboratory study of human skin biopsies reported regenerative effects of one specific spring water (Comano) on wound healing ex vivo, which concerns that water applied to skin, not drinking.[5]

timeline.event: Bottling begins at Holy Well, Malvern, UK.[2]
